p: I'm Kuzey Aydın. I'm a Windborn. Three of the seven great winds live inside me now, and they argue at three in the morning.

The North Wind, the Yıldız, from Istanbul. The Black Wind, the Karayel, from an ice cave in Iceland. And the southeast wind, the Keşişleme, from a hall under the paws of the Sphinx in Egypt, where I answered a riddle nobody had answered in five thousand years. (The answer was the wind. It's always the wind.)

Mordecai Vane, the man with the hand of gray stone, has only one: the Lodos, which his son Vex took from me on Crete. Mordecai still holds my grandmother prisoner in a gray tower, hidden in fog, far in the north.
So the score is three to one. To us.
But something has changed. In Egypt, Vera Vane, Mordecai's daughter, stood up to her brother to save my cousin Ela. She can't go home now. She's one of us.
And she told us something terrible. Her father is going to Japan to find the next Key, the Gündoğusu, the wind of the sunrise.
And this time, he's going himself.
**Kuzey Aydın,** 11. A Windborn with three winds. Can make rainbows. Cannot yet fly. Yet.
**Ela Aydın,** 12. Kuzey's cousin. Keeper of the Clue Book. Has a secret code with Vera that nobody else is allowed to know.
**Bora Kaya,** 11. Kuzey's best friend. Beastspeaker. Has made friends with a Minotaur, a raven, a horse, a camel and about fifty cats.
**Vera Vane,** 13. Mordecai's daughter. Ran away to join us. Wears her mother's silver bracelet. Never takes it off.
**Uncle Tarık.** Ela's dad. Archaeologist. Has run out of airline miles.
**Grandma Nermin.** The Keeper. Still a prisoner. Still singing.
**Mordecai Vane,** the Gray Hand. Has one Key. And a small black screen with a blinking red dot on it.
**Vex Vane,** 13. Mordecai's son. His fingers are turning to stone. He knows about the red dot.

chapters.t: Chapter One: Toilet Seats to Tokyo
p: The flight from Cairo to Tokyo takes fourteen hours. We sat next to the toilets for every one of them.
"Toilet-seat professionals," said Bora, settling in with a bag of Egyptian sweets and a neck pillow shaped like a crocodile. "This is our natural home."

Every few minutes, the toilet door banged open and shut, and somebody squeezed past our knees. The toilet flushed with a sound like a jet engine. The smell drifted over us in little clouds. Ela put on a sleep mask and earplugs and pretended she was somewhere else. Uncle Tarık fell asleep in about four minutes and slept for nine hours, snoring, with his mouth open and a book called *Myths and Legends of Old Japan* on his chest.
Vera sat by the window. She had never been on a normal plane before.
"Never?" said Bora, amazed. "Not even once?"

"We always went through the fog," said Vera. She was pressed against the window, watching the desert slide away underneath us, gold and brown and endless. "My father doesn't like planes. Too many people. Too slow." She smiled a little. "I like it. You can see everything."

She watched out of the window for hours. The desert. Then the sea, blue and wrinkled. Then mountains, brown and huge. Then clouds. Then, as it got dark, the lights of cities, scattered across the ground like spilled glitter.
I watched her watching. I thought about what she'd said, in Egypt. *I want what you have. Friends that argue at three in the morning.*
She kept touching her bracelet. The silver one, with the little gray stone. Turning it around and around her wrist, without seeming to notice.
Somewhere over India, I fell asleep.

I dreamed of the wind. Not my three winds. A different one. A soft, warm, golden wind, coming from far in the east, from where the sun rises. It blew across a sea of clouds, and over a mountain covered in snow. And on the mountain, something was waiting for me. Something very big, and very old, with a bag on its back.
And something else was coming toward the mountain too. From the north. Through the fog.
Something cold.
I woke up with a jolt. The plane was dark and humming. Everyone was asleep. Even Vera, with her head against the window.
Except, at the window, the little gray stone in her bracelet was glinting in the light from the toilet sign.
*Click. Click. Click.*
I didn't hear it. Not then. Nobody could have heard it.
But somewhere very far away, on a small black screen in a gray tower, a red dot was moving east.
Tokyo is like Istanbul if Istanbul was a robot.
That's the only way I can describe it. Huge, and crowded, and busy, and loud, like Istanbul. But everything is clean. Everything is on time. Everything has a button. Everything lights up.

We came out of the train station into a street so bright that it looked like daytime, even though it was nine o'clock at night. Giant screens on the sides of the buildings, showing ads for drinks and phones and cartoon characters. Neon signs in red and pink and blue and green, with Japanese letters that looked like little drawings. Thousands of people crossing the road all at the same time, from every direction at once, at a huge crossing where all the lights went green together, and somehow nobody bumped into anybody.
"Whoa," said Bora.

There were vending machines on every corner. Not just for drinks. For hot drinks and cold drinks, in the same machine. For soup. For noodles. For umbrellas. For socks. Bora found one that sold hot corn soup in a can, and bought six.
"This country," he said, holding six cans of hot soup, his eyes shining, "understands me."

We stayed in a tiny hotel where the rooms were the size of a wardrobe. Really. Uncle Tarık and I could touch both walls at the same time with our arms out. The bed filled the whole room. The bathroom was a sort of plastic pod, with a toilet that had more buttons than a TV remote. Bora pressed all of them, one at a time, and screamed three times.
Then we went out to eat.

We went to a restaurant where the food went around on a little conveyor belt, past all the seats, on tiny plates. Sushi, and little bowls of noodles, and fried things on sticks, and things none of us could recognize. You just took what you wanted off the belt as it went past, and at the end, they counted your plates.
Bora took twenty-three plates.

He would have taken more, but the man behind the counter came over and asked very politely, through Vera (who spoke a little Japanese, it turned out; she'd had a tutor), if Bora was "perhaps a professional eating champion." Bora said no, he was just hungry. The man bowed very deeply and brought him a free bowl of ice cream "out of respect."
Ela had the Clue Book open on the counter, between the soy sauce and a little pot of green tea.

"Okay," she said. "The star on the map is near Mount Fuji. But the map also has a tiny drawing next to it. Like the split rock in Iceland." She showed us. It was so small you could barely see it. A little arch. Like a gate. With two posts and two crossbars across the top. And beside it, a tiny animal with a pointed face and a big tail.
"That's a torii," said Vera. "A Japanese gate. They're at the entrance to shrines. Holy places. And the animal is a fox."
§CLUE A tiny drawing on the leather map, next to Japan's star: a gate, and a fox with a big tail.

"A fox and a gate," said Uncle Tarık. He was reading *Myths and Legends of Old Japan* very fast. "A fox and a gate. Wait. Wait! Here." He held up the book. "Fushimi Inari! In Kyoto! A shrine to the god Inari, who looks after rice and good fortune. It has thousands of gates. Thousands! Red ones! And the messengers of Inari are foxes. There are fox statues everywhere."
"Kyoto," said Ela, writing. "How far is that?"
"Two hours," said Vera. "On the bullet train."
Bora looked up from his ice cream. "There's a *bullet* train?"

chapters.t: Chapter Three: The Wind of Tokyo
p: That first night in Tokyo, in our tiny hotel room the size of a wardrobe, I couldn't sleep.

Uncle Tarık was snoring on the other side of the bed, his feet sticking out of the end of it. Through the wall, I could hear Bora snoring too, in the next wardrobe. And outside, the city hummed. Even at three in the morning. Trains and cars and the buzz of the giant screens and the soft electric hum of millions of lights.
I opened the window. Just a crack. It was the kind of window that only opens a crack.
The wind of Tokyo came in.

It wasn't like any wind I had met before. It was fast. Very fast. And busy. It zoomed in through the crack, swirled once around the tiny room, and zoomed out again, all in about one second. Like a person late for a train.
*Windborn,* it said, very quickly, on its way past. *Welcome. Sorry. Busy. Very busy. Many buildings. Many streets. Must hurry.*
"Wait," I said. "Please. Just for a second."
The wind stopped. Halfway out of the window. As if it was surprised.
*You want to talk?* it said. *To me? Nobody talks to me. Everybody is too busy. Like me.*
"I just wanted to say hello," I said.

The wind thought about that for a moment. Then it came back in, very slowly, and swirled around the room again. Gently, this time. It lifted the corner of the curtain. It rustled the map on the little table. It touched my face.
*Hello,* it said. More slowly. *Hello, Windborn. You are very far from home.*
"Yes," I said. "We're looking for my grandmother. And a Key. Near the big mountain."
*Fuji,* said the wind of Tokyo. Its voice changed. *The god of wind lives there. The old one. With the bag.* A pause. *We are all a little bit afraid of him. He is very loud.*
I laughed.

*And there is something else,* said the wind, quieter now. *Something the old winds are whispering about. In the north. A cold thing. Coming through the fog. The little winds are frightened. They are hiding in the alleys.*
"I know," I said. "I'm sorry. I'm going to try to stop it."
The wind of Tokyo swirled around me one more time. Very gently.
*Thank you for stopping,* it said. *To say hello. Nobody ever stops.*
Then it zoomed out of the window, and away over the rooftops, toward the lights, busy again, late for something.
I lay down on the tiny bed and fell asleep almost straight away.

The bullet train is called the Shinkansen, and it's the best thing ever invented. Bora said that. Then Ela said that. Then Uncle Tarık said that. Then even Vera said that, very quietly, with her face pressed against the window.

It's long and white and pointed at the front, like a giant bird's beak, and it goes so fast that the world outside turns into a blur. Three hundred kilometers an hour. Faster than a racing car. But inside, it's completely quiet and smooth. You could stand a coin on its edge on the table and it wouldn't fall over. Bora tried it. It didn't fall over.

A lady came along the aisle with a little trolley, selling lunch boxes. They're called bento. Little wooden boxes with lots of tiny compartments, each with something different in it. Rice shaped like a panda. A tiny fish. Pickled things in pink and yellow and green. An egg rolled up like a carpet. Bora bought four.
And then, about forty minutes out of Tokyo, Vera said, "Look."
We looked.
Out of the window, on the right, rising up over the houses and the fields and the hills, was a mountain.

But not like any mountain I had ever seen. It was perfect. A perfect cone, smooth and even on both sides, like a child's drawing of a mountain. Blue-gray at the bottom. White at the top, covered in snow. Standing all alone, with nothing else around it, like a king. A thin wisp of cloud was wrapped around its top like a scarf.
"Mount Fuji," whispered Ela.
The whole train went quiet. Even the Japanese people, who must have seen it a thousand times, were looking out of the windows. Some of them were taking photos.

"It's a volcano," said Uncle Tarık softly. "Sleeping. It last erupted three hundred years ago. It's the most sacred mountain in Japan. People have been climbing it for a thousand years, as a pilgrimage. Poets have written about it. Painters have painted it, over and over." He sighed. "Hokusai painted it thirty-six times."
"Why thirty-six?" said Bora.
"Because thirty-five wasn't enough," said Uncle Tarık.
I pressed my face against the window and looked at the mountain.
And the wind of the mountains spoke to me.

It was nothing like the other winds. Not chatty like the Greek ones. Not rumbling like the Icelandic ones. Not whispering secrets like the desert. It was soft, and polite, and very, very formal. It spoke in short, careful sentences. Like someone bowing before every word.
*Welcome, Windborn,* it said. *You have traveled far. We are honored.*
"Thank you," I whispered. "Um. I'm honored too."

*The god of wind will see you,* said the polite wind. *On the mountain. If you are worthy.* A pause. *But first, you must learn to reach the mountain. A Windborn who cannot fly cannot meet the god of wind.*
"Fly?" I said, out loud.
Everyone on the train looked at me. I sank down in my seat.
*Follow the fox,* said the polite wind. *The fox will show you. And Windborn.*
"Yes?"
The wind paused for a long time. When it spoke again, it was quieter. Worried.
*There is a cold thing coming. From the north. Through the fog. A cold thing with a stone hand. It walks the fog roads. We cannot stop it. Be quick, Windborn. Be very quick.*
Then it was gone.
I sat back in my seat. The mountain slid away behind us, white and perfect.
"Kuzey?" said Vera. "You've gone a funny color."
"Your father," I said quietly. "He's coming. Through the fog."
Vera's face went white. Her hand went to her bracelet. She turned it around her wrist, once, twice, three times.
She didn't say anything.
In Kyoto, we stayed in a ryokan.

A ryokan is a traditional Japanese inn, Vera explained. Very old. Made of wood and paper. You take your shoes off at the door, and you wear slippers inside, and different slippers in the bathroom, and you must never, ever wear the bathroom slippers outside the bathroom. Bora did this twice, and the lady who ran the ryokan, the Okami-san, followed him down the corridor making small, polite, horrified noises until he changed them.

Our rooms had floors covered in tatami mats, which are thick mats made of woven straw, that smell like hay and summer. There were no beds. At night, the Okami-san came in and laid out futons on the floor, thick soft mattresses with heavy quilts. The walls were sliding doors made of wood and paper. When the moon was out, it shone through the paper and made the whole room glow white.
And there was a garden.

It was the most peaceful place I have ever been. A tiny garden in the middle of the inn, with a little pond full of orange and white fish, a stone lantern covered in moss, a twisted pine tree and a bamboo pipe that slowly filled with water, and then tipped over, *tok,* and emptied, and filled again. *Tok.* Every minute or so. *Tok.*
I sat by the pond in the evening, in my cotton robe, which the Okami-san had given us all to wear, listening to the *tok.*
Uncle Tarık came and sat next to me. He was wearing his robe too, which was too short for him, and his bare ankles stuck out.
"You're worried," he said.
"He's coming," I said. "Mordecai. Himself. Not Vex. Not the Grays. Him." I looked at the fish. "In the northern lights, in Iceland, he talked to me. Did I tell you that?"
Uncle Tarık looked at me sharply. "No. You didn't tell me that."
So I told him. The face in the sky. The voice. *It feels like being outside a house, in the cold, looking through the window at a family having dinner. Forever.*
Uncle Tarık was quiet for a long time after I finished.
"I met him once," he said finally.
I stared at him.

"Mordecai. When I was a boy. Ten, maybe. He was Mum's student, then. He came to our flat every Tuesday, for tea, and they talked for hours about the winds and the old books. I didn't understand any of it. I thought he was boring." Uncle Tarık smiled a strange, sad smile. "But one Tuesday, he saw me trying to fix my kite. It was broken. The string was all tangled. And he sat down on the floor with me, for an hour, and untangled it. Very patiently. Knot by knot. He didn't say anything. He just did it. And then he took me up to the roof and flew it with me."
"Mordecai Vane," I said. "Flew a kite with you."
"He was very good at it," said Uncle Tarık. "He knew exactly how to hold the string so the wind would catch it." He shook his head. "I had forgotten all about it. Until now."
The bamboo pipe filled with water, and tipped over. *Tok.*

"People aren't just one thing, Kuzey," said Uncle Tarık quietly. "That's the thing about history. That's the thing about archaeology. You dig down, and down, and you find layers. A layer of fire. A layer of peace. A layer of war. A layer of a city. A layer of a farm. All in the same place. One on top of another."
He stood up, with a creak of knees.
"Mordecai has a layer of a young man who untangled a kite for a boy he didn't even know," he said. "It's still in there. Somewhere. Under all the ice."
He went back inside.
I sat by the pond for a long time, watching the orange fish in the dark water, and listening to the *tok.*
Ela said we needed a day.

"One day," she said, at breakfast in the ryokan, sitting on the tatami floor with a tray of fish and rice and pickles and miso soup in front of her. "To research. To plan. Fushimi Inari is huge. We need to know what we're looking for before we go in. And Dad needs to read his whole book."
"I've read half," said Uncle Tarık.
"Then you need to read the other half," said Ela.
So Ela and Uncle Tarık stayed in the ryokan, with books and maps and the Clue Book spread out across the tatami. And Vera took Bora and me to Nara.

Nara is a little city near Kyoto. It was the capital of Japan more than a thousand years ago. It has huge old temples, and a giant bronze Buddha as tall as a house, in a wooden hall so big it's one of the biggest wooden buildings in the world.
And it has deer.

Hundreds of them. More than a thousand. Wild deer, small and brown, with white spots on their backs, wandering freely all over the city. In the parks. In the streets. Outside the shops. In front of the temples. They've lived there for a thousand years, Vera said. People believed they were messengers of the gods. They're protected. Nobody is allowed to hurt them.
And they bow.
Really. If you bow to a deer in Nara, the deer bows back. A little nod of its head. People sell special crackers to feed them, and the deer have learned that if they bow, they get a cracker.
Bora bought fifty crackers.

Within about ten seconds, he was surrounded. Deer everywhere. Pushing their noses into his pockets. Nibbling his coat. Bowing and bowing and bowing, all at once, like a crowd of very polite, very hungry people.
"Okay, okay!" Bora was laughing. "One at a time! One at a time! Please! There's enough for everyone!"
He bowed to them. They bowed to him. He gave them crackers. They bowed again.
Then he stopped laughing.
He was listening to one of the deer. An old one, with a gray face and a torn ear. It was standing very close to him, looking up at him with big dark eyes, and it wasn't asking for crackers anymore.
"What's it saying?" I asked.
Bora's face had gone serious.

"She says," he said slowly, "that the deer can smell the weather. All animals can. And she says there's something wrong with the weather. Since last night. There's a fog coming. From the north. A strange fog. It doesn't smell like normal fog. It smells cold. Like metal. Like a fridge." He listened again. "She says the birds have stopped singing near the mountain. The big mountain. Fuji. She says the foxes are worried. The foxes are always worried, she says, but this time they're *really* worried."
Vera had gone very still.
"The fog road," she said quietly. "He's coming through the fog road."
The old deer bowed to Bora. A long, slow, serious bow. Not for a cracker. Then she turned and walked away into the trees.
Bora gave the rest of his crackers to the other deer, very quickly, and we went back to Kyoto on the first train.
On the train, Vera sat by the window and didn't say anything. She kept touching her bracelet.
"How did he know?" Bora asked me quietly, when she wasn't listening. "How does he always know where we're going? Before we even get there?"
I didn't have an answer.
But I looked at Vera's wrist. And for the first time, just for a second, something flickered in the back of my mind. Something small. Something about a stone that was always cold.
Then the train went into a tunnel, and the thought went away.
That evening, Uncle Tarık came back to the ryokan with a kite.

He had bought it in a little shop near the river. It was a Japanese kite, made of paper stretched over thin bamboo sticks, painted with the face of a warrior. A fierce red face, with big eyes and a black mustache. Like a samurai. Or a tengu.
"It's for flying," he said, a bit embarrassed, when we all stared at him.
"We know it's for flying, Dad," said Ela. "Why did you buy it?"

Uncle Tarık looked at me. I had told him, in the garden by the pond, about the face in the northern lights. He had told me about Mordecai untangling his kite, on the floor of Grandma's flat, when he was ten years old.
"I just wanted to," he said.

So we went down to the river. The Kamo River runs through the middle of Kyoto, wide and shallow and clear, with grassy banks where people walk their dogs and ride their bikes and sit and watch the water. There are stepping stones across it, in the shape of turtles. The sun was going down. The mountains around the city were turning purple.
Uncle Tarık unrolled the string and held the kite up.
There wasn't much wind. Just a little evening breeze, coming down the river.
The kite went up a few meters, wobbled, spun around and crashed into the grass.

He tried again. It crashed again. He tried a third time. It went up, caught the breeze, rose higher, and then the string got tangled around Uncle Tarık's arm, and his glasses, and his umbrella, and the kite fell on a man walking his dog, who said something very polite in Japanese that was clearly not polite at all.
"I'm very bad at this," said Uncle Tarık, untangling himself.
"Do you want me to help?" I said. "With the wind?"
He thought about it. Then he shook his head.
"No," he said. "Thank you. I want to do it myself. Like I did when I was ten." He looked at the tangled string in his hands. "He showed me how. I just have to remember."
He sat down on the grass, and very patiently, knot by knot, he started to untangle the string.
I sat down next to him and watched. So did Ela. Bora went off to talk to a heron that was standing in the river. Vera sat a little way off, watching too.

It took him a long time. The string was very tangled. But Uncle Tarık didn't hurry. He didn't get frustrated. He just did it, one knot at a time, with his tongue sticking out of the corner of his mouth, exactly like Ela does.

"He held the string like this," Uncle Tarık said quietly, when he was finished. He stood up and held the string in a loop around two fingers. "Loose. Not tight. He said if you hold it too tight, you can't feel what the wind wants. You have to let the kite tell you."
He held up the kite and let it go.

The breeze caught it. Uncle Tarık let out the string, slowly, holding it loose. The kite rose. Wobbled. Rose again. He let out more string, and more. Higher. Higher. Until the fierce red samurai face was dancing high above the river, against the purple sky, with the first stars coming out around it.
Uncle Tarık stood on the riverbank, holding the string, looking up at it. His face looked very young.
I didn't help. I didn't ask the wind for anything. I didn't need to.
*He knows how,* said the North Wind, inside me, softly. *Someone taught him well.*
Vera came and stood next to me.
"My father," she said quietly, watching the kite. "He used to fly kites with us. On the beach. On Sundays. Before." She swallowed. "I forgot. I'd forgotten all about it until right now."
Nobody said anything.
The kite danced above the river until it was dark. Then Uncle Tarık wound it in, very carefully, and carried it back to the ryokan under his arm, like something precious.
The fox statue was looking at me. I was sure of it.

It sat on a stone pedestal beside the path, a red bib around its neck and a key carved in its mouth. Behind it, the path climbed up the mountain through a tunnel of bright orange gates, one after another after another, so close together that they made a glowing orange hallway that went on forever.

"Fushimi Inari," said Uncle Tarık, reading from his guidebook. "There are about ten thousand gates, called torii. People donate them for good luck. Each one has the name of the person who gave it, written on the back in black letters. The foxes are the messengers of the god Inari. The key in this fox's mouth is the key to the rice storehouse."
"Ten thousand," said Bora. "That's a lot of doors to walk through without going anywhere."

It was very early morning. We had come at dawn, before the tourists, because Ela said so. The mountain was misty and quiet. Only a few old people with walking sticks were climbing the path ahead of us, and a man sweeping leaves with a broom made of twigs.

The gates were incredible. Bright orange-red, the color of a fire, with black bases and black tops. They glowed in the early light, so that walking through them was like walking through a tunnel made of sunset. Some of them were huge and old, with cracked paint. Some of them were small and new and shiny. They went up the mountain in two long lines, side by side, twisting and turning, up stone steps, around corners, into the forest.
Vera walked at the back, saying nothing. She had been quiet since the train. Sometimes she looked at her phone, then quickly put it away. Sometimes she touched her bracelet.
The wind in Japan was soft, polite and very formal. It came down the tunnel of gates in little gusts, making the paper prayers tied to the gates rustle and flutter.
*Welcome, Windborn. You have come. Follow the fox.*
"Follow the fox," I said.
"Which fox?" asked Ela. "There are about five hundred of them."

She was right. There were fox statues everywhere. Big ones and small ones, old ones covered in moss and new ones with bright white paint. Foxes with keys in their mouths. Foxes with jewels. Foxes with scrolls. Foxes sitting, foxes standing, foxes with red bibs and foxes without. They sat at every corner, on every wall, beside every little shrine, watching us with their narrow stone eyes.
"How are we supposed to know which one?" said Bora. "They all look the same."
"They don't, actually," said Ela, peering at one. "This one has a chipped ear. And that one..."
Then one of the stone foxes jumped off its pedestal.

It wasn't stone anymore. It landed on the path in front of us without a sound. A real fox. White as snow, white as paper, with a long pointed face and black-tipped ears. And *three tails,* swishing behind it like white flames. Its eyes were gold, like coins.
It looked at us. One by one. Its gold eyes rested on Bora longest.
Then it turned and trotted up the path, between the orange gates, and disappeared into the mist.
"Bora," I said.
"I know, I know." Bora ran after it. "Hey! Excuse me! Mr. Fox! Ms. Fox? Can we talk?"
From the mist, a voice answered. Not out loud. But Bora heard it. A sly, amused voice, like someone laughing behind their hand.
Bora stopped so suddenly that Ela crashed into him.
"What did it say?" she asked, rubbing her nose.
Bora's face went pink.
"It said," he said, "'The big one is cute. Hurry up, little humans. The god of wind does not like to wait.'" He swallowed. "'And the cold man is already in Japan.'"
The white fox's name was Shiro, which means *white,* and she was a kitsune. A fox spirit. Three hundred years old.

Bora says she's very proud of her third tail. She mentioned it five times in the first ten minutes. Kitsune grow a new tail every hundred years, she said, and the ones with nine tails are the most powerful creatures in Japan, and she was going to have nine one day, and then everyone would see.
"She says," Bora translated, "that a three-tailed fox is very rare and impressive. And that she's very beautiful. And that I should tell everyone."
"She *is* very beautiful," said Vera.
Shiro looked at Vera with her gold eyes, and swished her three tails, and looked very pleased.

She led us up the mountain through the endless orange gates. Past little shrines with stone foxes, and stone lanterns, and stacks of tiny orange gates that people had left as offerings, like toys. Past waterfalls, and bamboo forests that creaked in the wind, and tiny cats sleeping on steps. Past old graves covered in moss, with incense burning in front of them, the smoke curling up into the mist.
The higher we climbed, the more the mist thickened. Until we could only see the next gate ahead of us. And the next. And the next.
And then something strange happened.
We came around a corner, and there was a fox statue with a chipped ear. The same one Ela had pointed at, at the very bottom of the mountain.
"That's impossible," said Ela. "We passed that one an hour ago. At the start."
We kept climbing. Around another corner. Up some steps. Through twenty more gates.
And there was the fox with the chipped ear. Again.
"We're going in circles," said Uncle Tarık. He looked around at the mist. "But we can't be. We've been going *up* the whole time."
Shiro sat down in the middle of the path, with her three tails wrapped around her feet. She looked at us. Her gold eyes were full of laughter.
"Bora," I said. "What's she doing?"

Bora listened. He frowned. "She says it's a test. She says kitsune are tricksters. They love games. She says the path is enchanted. It goes round and round forever, through the gates, until you find the way out. Most people never do. They just walk and walk until they give up and go home." Bora listened again. "She says, 'If you can't find the way out of my gates, little humans, you are not clever enough to meet the god of wind. Good luck!'"
Shiro swished her tails and disappeared into the mist.
We stood there, in the tunnel of orange gates, in the fog. The fox with the chipped ear watched us with its stone eyes.
"Great," said Bora. "Just great. We're going to walk through gates for the rest of our lives."
"No, we're not," said Ela.
She had the Clue Book out, and her pencil, and the look on her face. The look she gets when she's about to solve something.

"Every gate," she said slowly, "has a name written on the back. The name of the person who donated it. Dad said so." She walked to the nearest gate and looked at the back of it. Black Japanese letters, painted on the orange wood. "Vera. Can you read these?"
"Some of them," said Vera. "My tutor taught me."
"Then read them," said Ela. "All of them. As we go."

chapters.t: Chapter Ten: The Gate With Her Name
p: So we walked, and Vera read.

It was slow. Some of the gates had long names, and some of the paint was old and faded, and some of the letters Vera didn't know. Ela wrote down every name she could read in the Clue Book, in a long list. *Tanaka Corporation. Yamamoto family. Kyoto Rice Company. Suzuki Hiroshi, 1997.* Gate after gate after gate.
We came around the corner to the fox with the chipped ear.
"Again," said Bora miserably.
"Good," said Ela. "Keep going. Keep reading."
Vera kept reading. Ela kept writing. *Tanaka Corporation. Yamamoto family. Kyoto Rice Company. Suzuki Hiroshi, 1997.*
Ela stopped.

"They're the same," she said. "The same names. In the same order. Look." She showed us the Clue Book. Two lists, side by side. Exactly the same. "The path is a loop. A circle. We've been walking around the same forty-nine gates over and over."
"Forty-nine," I said. "Seven times seven."
"Of course," said Ela. "It's always seven with the Order."
"So how do we get out of a circle?" said Uncle Tarık.
Ela was frowning at the list. Running her pencil down it. Up. Down again.

"There's one name I don't understand," said Vera suddenly. She was pointing at a gate. A small one, old, its orange paint faded almost to pink. The writing on the back was different from the others. Not the usual Japanese letters. A different kind. "It's in katakana. That's the alphabet the Japanese use for foreign words. Foreign names." She traced the letters with her finger, sounding them out. "Ne... ru... mi... n. A... i... dou... n."
She looked up.
"Nermin Aydın," she said. "1983."
§CLUE Forty-nine gates in a loop. One of them has a foreign name on the back: Nermin Aydın, 1983. Walk through it the wrong way.
Nobody breathed.
I walked up to the little faded gate. I put my hand on the old wood. It was warm. Warmer than it should have been. And I could feel her. Very faint. Like the smell of cinnamon in an empty kitchen.
"She was here," I said. "She gave a gate."
"So that's the way out," said Bora. "We go through Grandma's gate!"
"We've already gone through it," said Ela. "Twice. Nothing happened." She bit her pencil. "There has to be something different. Something about how you go through it."
I looked at the gate. At the front, which was plain orange. At the back, where the name was written.
All the other gates, we had walked through from the front. Every single one. Up the mountain. Reading the names on the back as we passed.
"Backwards," I said. "We have to go through it backwards. The other way. Facing her name."
Ela's eyes went wide. "Down the mountain, instead of up," she said. "Against the flow. Kitsune are tricksters. The trick is to go the wrong way."
So we turned around. We walked past Grandma's gate, up the path a little way. Then we turned back, and walked down toward it. Facing her name, painted on the old wood in her careful letters.
Nermin Aydın. 1983.
We walked through it.
And the mist vanished.

We were standing on a wooden platform at the top of the mountain. In bright sunlight. The orange gates were behind us, and the path, and the forest. And Shiro the fox was sitting on the railing, her three tails swishing, her gold eyes laughing.
"She says," said Bora, laughing too, "'Took you long enough.'"

The platform stood at the edge of a cliff. Below us, a sea of clouds stretched out in every direction, white and soft and endless, like a giant had spread cotton wool over the whole world. The sun was shining down on it, and it glowed.
And far away, rising above the clouds like a white island in a white sea, was a perfect cone-shaped mountain with snow on its top.
"Mount Fuji," whispered Ela.
Shiro jumped down off the railing and sat in front of us. She looked at me with her gold eyes for a long time. Then she spoke to Bora.

"The god of wind lives there," Bora translated. "On the summit. His name is Fūjin. He carries all the winds of the east in a great bag on his shoulders. And his brother, Raijin, the god of thunder, beats a drum that makes the storms." Shiro flicked her three tails. "Fūjin has been guarding the sunrise wind for the Order for eight hundred years. He will test you, Windborn. He tests everyone."
"How far is it?" asked Uncle Tarık, looking at the distant mountain. "By train?"
Shiro laughed. A sharp, yapping fox laugh.
"Train?" said Bora. "She says, 'Silly human. Nobody takes the train to meet a god. The wind will carry you.'" He listened. "'If you can fly.'"
Everyone looked at me.
"I can't fly," I said.
"You can do almost everything else," said Ela. "Snow. Clouds. Sandstorms. Rainbows."

"Those are all things the *wind* does," I said. "Not me. I ask, and the wind does them. Flying is different. Flying is me." I looked at the drop, down into the clouds. It was very, very far. "I lifted myself about ten centimeters off a bed once. In Cairo. For about two seconds. Then I fell off and hit my head on the wall."
Shiro said something.

"She says," said Bora, "that's why we can't go yet. She says a Windborn must learn to fly before he can meet Fūjin. Otherwise he'll fall into the clouds and that will be very embarrassing for everyone. Especially her. Because she brought us."
"Then how do I learn?" I said.
Shiro looked toward the north. Toward a line of dark green mountains, covered in forest, on the far side of the city.

"Kurama," said Bora. "She says there's a mountain called Kurama. With a forest of very old trees. And in the forest, there are teachers." He frowned. "She says they have very long noses. And wings. And very bad tempers."
Uncle Tarık looked up from his book. His face had gone pale.
"Tengu," he said.
"Tengu," said Uncle Tarık, on the little train that took us up into the mountains north of Kyoto, "are some of the strangest creatures in Japanese legend."
He had his book open on his knees. He looked nervous. Uncle Tarık is not usually nervous about legends. He usually gets excited about them.

"They live in the mountains. In the deep forests. They're part bird and part man. Some of them have the heads of crows, with beaks. Those are the young ones. The older, more powerful ones have red faces and very, very long noses." He held up a picture. A man with a bright red face, a fierce frown, wild white hair and a nose as long as a carrot, sticking straight out. He wore the robes of a mountain monk, and he had huge black feathered wings on his back. "They're proud. Very proud. And they can be dangerous. In the old stories, they kidnap people who insult them. Or play terrible tricks on them."
"Great," said Bora. "Love that. Very welcoming."

"But," said Uncle Tarık, "they are also the greatest teachers in Japan. Of sword-fighting. Of magic. Of flying." He turned the page. "The most famous story is about a boy called Ushiwakamaru. A thousand years ago, he was sent to live in the temple on Mount Kurama. And at night, he sneaked out into the forest. And the King of the Tengu, Sōjōbō, taught him to fight. And to leap. And to fly through the treetops. And he became the greatest warrior in Japan."
Shiro, who was sitting in Bora's lap pretending to be a normal white dog (with one tail; she could hide the other two), yawned.
"She says the story is mostly true," said Bora. "She says Sōjōbō exaggerates his part."
The train climbed up and up through the mountains, through forests of tall dark trees. It was colder up here. The leaves on some of the trees had turned red and orange, like fire.
At the top, there was a little village with wooden houses and a temple. And above the temple, a path that went up into the forest.

The forest on Mount Kurama is the oldest forest I have ever seen. The trees are cedars. Huge ones, so tall that you have to lean back to see the tops, so thick that five people holding hands couldn't reach around them. Their trunks are dark red and stringy, and their branches are dark green and feathery, and they block out the sky. It's dim in there, even in the middle of the day. Green and dim and quiet, like being underwater.
And the roots.

The roots of the cedars come up out of the ground. Huge, twisted, knotted roots, spreading across the path like giant snakes, like the fingers of a buried giant. You have to climb over them. There's a famous path through the forest called the Path of Roots, and that's all it is. Roots, roots and more roots, twisting together.
"Ushiwakamaru practiced here," said Uncle Tarık quietly. "Leaping from root to root. At night."
I stopped in the middle of the Path of Roots, and listened.
The wind in the forest was different from the polite wind of the city. It was wild and fast and sharp. It whistled through the tops of the cedars, high above us, very fast. It laughed.
And then a voice came out of the trees above us.
"WHO," it said, "DARES TO WALK ON THE ROOTS OF KURAMA?"

chapters.t: Chapter Thirteen: The King of the Tengu
p: They came down out of the trees all at once.

Dozens of them. Dropping out of the dark green branches on huge black wings, landing on the roots around us with soft thumps. The young ones had the heads of crows, black and glossy, with sharp beaks and clever eyes, wearing little black caps and the white robes of mountain monks. They hopped from root to root, cawing and clacking their beaks.
And in the middle of them, landing last, on the biggest root of all, was the King.
Sōjōbō.

He was twice as tall as Uncle Tarık. His face was bright red, as red as a tomato, with fierce white eyebrows and a long white beard that went down to his belt. His nose was enormous. As long as my arm. It stuck straight out of his face like a branch. His wings were huge and black and ragged at the edges, and when he folded them, they wrapped around him like a cloak. He wore the robes of a mountain monk, white and orange, with big pompoms on the front. And he carried a fan made of feathers, as big as a door.
He looked down his enormous nose at us.
"Children," he said, in a voice like a landslide. "And a fox. And a man with a book." He sniffed. Very loudly. With his very long nose. "Who smells of fear and pickles."
"That's me," said Uncle Tarık weakly. "The pickles. From the train."
Sōjōbō ignored him. His fierce eyes moved to me. Then they narrowed.

"You," he said. "You have winds inside you. Three of them. I can smell them. The north, the black, the desert." He leaned down, very close, until the tip of his giant nose was almost touching my forehead. "What are you?"
"I'm a Windborn," I said. My voice was shaking. "My name is Kuzey Aydın. I need to learn to fly. So I can meet Fūjin. On Mount Fuji. Shiro brought me."
Sōjōbō looked at Shiro. Shiro looked back at him, swishing all three of her tails, very unimpressed.
"The three-tailed fox," said Sōjōbō, "is a very annoying creature."
Shiro yapped something.
"She says," Bora translated, "'And you are a very old crow with a carrot on your face.'"
There was a terrible silence.
All the crow-headed tengu went very still. Sōjōbō's red face went even redder. His eyebrows came down. His wings opened, slowly, huge and black, until they blocked out the whole forest.
Then he threw back his head and laughed.
It was a huge laugh. It shook the trees. Pine needles rained down on us. All the crow-tengu started laughing too, cawing and clacking their beaks.

"Ha!" roared Sōjōbō. "A carrot! Three hundred years, and the fox still has the sharpest tongue in Kyoto!" He wiped his eyes with the end of his beard. Then he looked at me again, and his face was serious.
"A Windborn," he said. "The last one who came to me was a girl from Persia. Two thousand years ago. With a red scarf."
"Talos told me about her," I said. "In Crete. He said to tell her he remembered her song."
Sōjōbō went very still.
"You met Talos?" he said. "The bronze one? He is still alive?"
"He's resting now," I said. "He's free. My friend Bora pulled out the nail."
The King of the Tengu looked at Bora for a long time. Then he looked at me.

"Hm," he said. "Very well. I will teach you to fly, little Windborn." He raised his giant feather fan. "But be warned. It will hurt. It will be very, very embarrassing. And you will fall many, many times."
He was right.
It hurt. It was very, very embarrassing. And I fell many, many times.
The first lesson was on the Path of Roots. Sōjōbō made me stand on one root, and jump to another. Then another. Then another. Faster and faster.
"Not with your legs!" he roared, every time I jumped. "With the WIND! Ask the wind to carry you!"
I asked the wind to carry me. The wind carried me straight into a tree.
I asked again. The wind carried me straight up, about two meters, and then let go, and I fell flat on my back on a root. The crow-tengu laughed so hard that two of them fell out of a tree.
"AGAIN!" roared Sōjōbō.

I tried again. And again. And again. For hours. Until my arms and legs and back were covered in bruises, and there were pine needles in my hair, and I had fallen on every single root on the Path of Roots at least twice.

Ela sat on a root at the side, with the Clue Book, taking notes. Bora sat next to her, feeding peanuts to the crow-tengu, who it turned out loved peanuts more than anything. Vera sat a little apart, watching. Uncle Tarık had found a fallen tree with interesting carvings on it, and was lying on the ground under it, examining them with a flashlight.
"I can't do it," I said, lying on my back on a root for the fiftieth time, looking up at the cedars. "I can't. It's not working."
Sōjōbō landed on the root next to me, his wings folding. He looked down his long nose at me.
"Why not?" he said.
"I don't know! I ask the wind, and it lifts me, and then it drops me. Or it throws me. Or it pushes me into a tree. It won't just... hold me."
"Hm," said Sōjōbō. He sat down on the root, his robes spreading out around him. He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "When you ask the wind to make snow, what do you do?"
"I ask it. Nicely. And it makes snow."
"And when you ask it to lift you?"
"I ask it," I said. "Nicely. And..." I stopped.
"And?" said Sōjōbō.
"And I hold on," I said slowly. "I hold on really, really tight. Because I'm scared I'll fall."
"Ah," said the King of the Tengu.

He stood up. He spread his huge black wings. And then, without flapping them at all, he rose up into the air. Slowly. Smoothly. Like a leaf on a breeze. Up and up, until he was hovering above me, between the cedar trunks, completely still.

"The wind cannot carry what will not let go," he said. "You are holding on to the ground with your whole heart, little Windborn. Your feet. Your fear. You ask the wind to carry you, and at the same time you are holding on to the earth with both hands. So the wind pulls, and you pull, and you both fall over." He floated down again and landed lightly beside me. "To fly, you must trust the wind more than you trust the ground."
§CLUE To fly, you must trust the wind more than you trust the ground. (Sōjōbō, King of the Tengu.)
I lay there on the root, looking up at the cedars.
*Trust the wind more than the ground.*
"Ela," I said. "Write that down."
"Already did," said Ela.

chapters.t: Chapter Fifteen: Meanwhile, on the Fog Road
p: *This part of the story was told to Kuzey much later. By Vex.*
The fog road was the coldest place in the world.

Vex walked through it behind his father. All around them, there was nothing but gray. Gray fog, thick and wet and freezing, so thick that he could barely see his father's back, two steps in front of him. There was no ground. There was no sky. There was only the fog, and the cold, and his father's footsteps, and the sound of his own breathing.
He hated the fog roads.

His father walked through them like he was walking down a street. Calmly. Not looking left or right. His long gray coat swirling around his legs. His stone hand held out in front of him, cracked and gray, with the Lodos Key in it, glowing dully. Showing the way.
The Lodos was screaming. Vex could hear it. A thin, high, endless scream, like a kettle that never stopped boiling. He had heard it every day for weeks.
"Father," said Vex.
"Mm."
"Does it hurt? Your hand? When the Key screams?"
His father didn't answer for a long time. They walked on through the gray.
"I told you," he said at last. "It stops hurting. After a while."
"But does it?" said Vex. "Really?"
His father didn't answer that at all.

In his coat pocket, Vex could feel the little black screen. His father had given it to him to carry. *Keep an eye on your sister,* he had said, and smiled. Every few minutes, Vex took it out and looked at it. A map of Japan. A red dot, in Kyoto. On a mountain north of the city.
Blinking. *Blink. Blink. Blink.*
Vera.
He thought about his sister on the stairs under the Sphinx. *I hear you crying at night, when you think I'm asleep.*
He thought about her on the stairs at the gray tower, holding his hands. The way their mother used to.

He thought about the bracelet. About his mother's face, two weeks before she died, giving it to Vera. *To keep you safe.* He had been there. He had been six. He had cried because he didn't get a bracelet, and his mother had laughed and given him her little silver compass instead.
He had lost the compass. Years ago. He had told everyone he didn't care.
He had cried for a week.
He looked at the red dot. *Blink. Blink. Blink.*
He could drop the screen. Right now. Into the fog. It would fall forever. His father would never find it.
His fingers closed around it in his pocket. His stone fingers. Hard and cold. Clicking.
He didn't drop it.
He was too afraid.

Ahead of him, his father stopped. The fog was thinning. Through it, Vex could see trees. Tall, dark trees. And below them, very far away, lights. A city. And beyond the city, rising above the clouds, a perfect white mountain.
"Japan," said Mordecai Vane softly. He looked down at the screen in Vex's hand. "And there she is. On Mount Kurama. With the tengu. How very clever of the boy."
He smiled.
"We'll wait for them on Fuji," he said. "Let the boy do all the hard work. As usual."

That night, we stayed in the temple on Mount Kurama. The monks let us sleep on the floor of a long wooden hall, on thin futons, under heavy blankets. It was cold. The wind whistled through the cracks in the old wooden walls.
I couldn't sleep. My whole body hurt. Every bruise had a bruise.
I lay on my back and looked at the dark ceiling, and tried to trust the wind more than the ground. It's very hard to do lying down.
Then I heard someone get up.
It was Vera. She went quietly to the sliding door at the end of the hall, opened it and went outside.
After a minute, I followed her.

She was sitting on the wooden steps of the temple, in the moonlight, looking out at the dark forest. Her arms were wrapped around her knees. She had her bracelet off. She was holding it in her hand, turning it over and over.
She jumped when I sat down next to her. Then she relaxed a little.
"Can't sleep?" she said.
"Bruises," I said.
She almost smiled. Then she looked back down at the bracelet.
"Kuzey," she said. "Can I ask you something? And you won't tell anyone?"
"Okay."

"If you had something," she said slowly. "Something that belonged to someone you loved. Someone who was gone. The only thing you had left of them. And you found out it was..." She stopped. "Wrong. Bad. Something bad was inside it. Would you throw it away?"
I didn't know what she meant. Not then. I thought she was talking about her father. About loving someone who had something bad inside him.
"I don't know," I said. "I think I'd try to get the bad thing out. And keep the rest."
Vera looked at me for a long time.
"Get the bad thing out," she said quietly. "And keep the rest."
She looked down at the bracelet in her hand. At the little gray stone. She put her thumbnail against the edge of the stone, as if she was going to try to pry it out.
Then she stopped.
Her hand was shaking.
"Not yet," she whispered. "I can't. Not yet."
She put the bracelet back on her wrist, and pulled her sleeve down over it, and stood up.
"Goodnight, Kuzey," she said. "Thank you."
She went back inside.
I sat on the steps for a long time, in the moonlight, not understanding.
I understand now. I wish I'd understood then. I wish I'd asked her what she meant. I wish I'd said, *Show me.*
But I didn't. I was eleven, and I was tired, and my bruises hurt, and I didn't understand.
Behind me, in the dark forest, something laughed. A sharp, clacking laugh, like a crow.
Then the wind came through the cedars, fast and wild, and went away again over the mountain.
At dawn, Sōjōbō took me to the top of the tallest cedar on Mount Kurama.

I don't know how tall it was. Taller than Galata Tower. Taller than anything. He carried me up there under one arm, like a bag of rice, flapping his huge black wings, and set me down on a branch near the very top, where the tree was thin and swaying in the wind.

Below me, very far below, I could see the temple roofs, and the Path of Roots, and four tiny dots that were Ela and Bora and Vera and Uncle Tarık, looking up. Beyond the forest, Kyoto spread out in the morning mist. And far, far away, rising above the clouds, Mount Fuji, pink in the sunrise.
I held onto the trunk of the tree with both arms. Very tightly.
"Let go," said Sōjōbō, hovering in the air beside me.
"No," I said.
"Let go, little Windborn."
"I'll fall."

"Yes," said Sōjōbō. "Probably. The first time. Then I will catch you, and bring you back up, and you will try again." His red face was very serious. "But you will not fly while you are holding the tree. You cannot hold the tree and the wind at the same time."
I looked down. My stomach turned over.

I thought about Bora, going down the fire stairs with his eyes shut, saying *I'm fine, I'm fine, I'm fine.* I thought about Bora in the Great Pyramid, holding the back of my shirt. Bora is afraid of heights. Bora does it anyway. Every time.
I thought about Grandma, standing up in a little boat in the middle of a storm, holding the mast, singing.
*Trust the wind more than the ground.*
I closed my eyes.
I listened.

The wind at the top of the cedar was fast and wild and cold. It whistled through the branches. It tugged at my clothes. It was the wind of the mountain tops. The wind the tengu flew on. It wasn't polite like the city wind. It was laughing. It was free.
*Come on, Windborn,* it said. *Come and play.*
And inside me, my three winds were quiet. Waiting. Watching. The North Wind. The Black Wind. The Keşişleme. For the first time, none of them said anything at all.
I let go of the tree.
I fell.
I fell for about one second. The longest second of my life. The wind rushing past my ears. My stomach in my throat. The ground rushing up, the cedar branches flashing past.
And in that second, I stopped holding on.

I stopped holding on to the ground. To my fear. To the tree, to the earth, to everything. I just... let go. Like falling asleep. Like floating on your back in the sea, the way Bora did in Crete, with his arms spread out and his eyes closed. Trusting the water to hold you up.
I trusted the wind to hold me up.
And it did.
I stopped falling.

I opened my eyes. I was floating. In the air. Between the cedar trees, halfway up, with nothing under me but empty space and the Path of Roots a long, long way down. The wind was under me, around me, holding me, like a giant hand. Like a hammock. Like being held by someone who loves you.
I wasn't falling.
I was *flying.*
Far below, I heard a scream. It was Ela. Then Bora shouting, "HE'S DOING IT! HE'S DOING IT!" Then Uncle Tarık, shouting something that wasn't words at all.
Sōjōbō floated down beside me, his wings spread wide. And for the first time since I met him, the King of the Tengu smiled.
"There," he said. "You see? Easy."
"*Easy?*" I said. "That wasn't easy!"
"No," Sōjōbō agreed. "It was very hard. The hardest thing. To let go." He tilted his head. "Now. Let's see if you can go *up.*"
I will remember that morning for the rest of my life.

Sōjōbō taught me for three hours. Up and down, between the cedars. Left and right. Fast and slow. How to turn, by leaning into the wind like a bird. How to stop, by asking the wind to hold still. How to land, softly, on a branch, on a root, on the temple roof. (I didn't land very softly on the temple roof. A monk came out and shouted at me. Sōjōbō shouted back at him. The monk went back inside.)

The crow-tengu flew with me, cawing and laughing, showing off, doing loops and dives. One of them, a young one called Karasu, who was about my age in tengu years, raced me between the trees. He won. Easily. But he said I was "not bad for a human," and gave me a black feather.
By the end of the morning, I could fly.
Not like a tengu. Not like a bird. Not fast, or very high, and I wobbled a lot, especially on the turns. But I could fly. Up, and down, and around, and land without falling over. Mostly.
When I came down at last and landed on the Path of Roots, in front of everyone, my legs were shaking so much that I sat down straight away.
Ela was crying. Again. She'd been crying a lot on this adventure. She kept saying it was the pollen.
"You flew," she said. "You actually flew. Like a person. Through the air."
"I know," I said. "I was there."
Bora picked me up off the ground in a huge hug, so hard that my feet left the ground again. "My best friend can FLY!" he shouted to the whole forest. "My best friend can FLY!"
The crow-tengu cawed. Shiro, sitting on a root, swished her three tails, looking very smug, as if it had all been her idea.
Sōjōbō landed in front of me and folded his great black wings.

"You are not finished," he said. "You are a beginner. A baby bird. You will need to practice every day for a hundred years." He paused. "But you are ready to meet Fūjin. I think. And Fūjin will be very surprised. He has not seen a Windborn fly in two thousand years." He sniffed. "Tell him Sōjōbō taught you. Tell him he still owes me money."
"I will," I said. "Thank you. Thank you so much."
The King of the Tengu looked at me for a long moment, down his enormous red nose.
Then he did something strange. He bowed. A small bow. Just his head.
"The girl with the red scarf," he said quietly. "Two thousand years ago. She was my best student. Until today." He straightened up. "Go. The fox is waiting. And the cold one is coming."
He spread his wings and rose up into the cedars and was gone.

That night, our last night at the temple on Mount Kurama, I couldn't sleep. Again. My head was full of the wind, and every time I closed my eyes, I felt myself falling and then floating, falling and then floating.
So I went outside. And I flew.

Only a little. Just up to the top of the temple roof, carefully, wobbling, and down again. Then to the top of a cedar. Then down again. Practicing, the way Sōjōbō had told me to. Every day for a hundred years.
On the third time up, something landed on the branch next to me.
Karasu. The young crow-tengu who had raced me. He had a black beak and bright black eyes and a little black cap, and he was wearing a white robe that was too big for him, so the sleeves flapped.
"Can't sleep, Windborn?" he said, in a voice like a rusty gate. The tengu could all talk. Not just to Bora. To everyone.
"No," I said.
"Me neither," said Karasu. "Want to see something?"
Before I could answer, he dropped off the branch and swooped away over the forest.
I followed him.

We flew over the dark cedars, over the mountain, out over the valley. The cold night air rushed past my face. My winds were laughing inside me. Below us, the forest gave way to fields, and then to houses, and then to the city.
Kyoto at night.

It spread out below us like a black velvet cloth covered in a million tiny lights. Golden lights in windows. Red lanterns outside temples. The bright white lights of the streets, in neat straight lines, like a giant grid. The river running through the middle, a ribbon of black, with the lights of the bridges reflected in it. And the temples. Hundreds of them. Their curved roofs glowing in the moonlight, and their pagodas, tall and thin, rising up like stacks of hats.

Karasu flew low over the city, and I followed him. Over a huge temple with a golden roof that shone in the moonlight like it was made of fire. Over a street of old wooden houses with paper lanterns, where a lady in a kimono was walking very slowly, with a parasol, in the middle of the night. Over a bamboo forest, the tall stalks swaying and creaking in the wind like a sea of green.
"Beautiful, yes?" said Karasu.
"Yes," I said. I couldn't say anything else.

We landed on the top of a pagoda. A tall, five-story wooden tower, very old, with a curved roof on every story and a long bronze spike on top. We sat on the very top roof, next to the spike, with the whole city spread out below us.
"The fox told us," said Karasu after a while. "About your grandmother. The cold man has her."
"Yes."
"He came to Kurama once," said Karasu. "A long time ago. Before I hatched. My grandfather told me. A young man. Very serious. He wanted Sōjōbō to teach him to fly."
I stared at him. "Mordecai? He came here?"

"Sōjōbō tried," said Karasu. "For a whole month. Every day. But the wind would not carry him. Not even a little. He fell every time. A hundred times. Two hundred." Karasu ruffled his feathers. "My grandfather said he never gave up. He was very brave. But the wind would not carry him. In the end, Sōjōbō told him to go home." He looked at me with his bright black eyes. "My grandfather said the young man cried. On the last day. On the Path of Roots. He thought nobody could see."
I didn't say anything for a long time.

I thought about Sōjōbō saying, *You are holding on to the ground with your whole heart.* I thought about a young man who wanted to fly more than anything, falling, and falling, and falling. Two hundred times.
"Why wouldn't the wind carry him?" I said.
Karasu shrugged his wings. "Sōjōbō says some people are holding on too tightly. To something. Something they're afraid to lose. And they can't let go. Not even to fly."
Far away, to the south, beyond the city and the mountains, I could see a line of white on the horizon, glowing faintly in the moonlight. Mount Fuji.
And around its top, very faint, I could see something else.
A thin gray wisp. Like a scarf. Like smoke.
Fog.
On a clear night. With no clouds anywhere else in the sky.
"He's there," I said. "Already."
Karasu followed my gaze. He ruffled his feathers again, uneasily.
"Then you'd better get some sleep, Windborn," he said. "Tomorrow you meet a god."
We flew back to Kurama together under the moon.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty: Over the Sea of Clouds
p: We went back to the platform at the top of Fushimi Inari the next afternoon. Through the orange gates, past the foxes, past Grandma's gate. This time, the path let us straight through. Shiro said that was "because the gates like you now."
At the top, the sea of clouds was still there, stretching out to the horizon. And Mount Fuji, white and perfect, floating above it.
I stood at the edge of the platform.
"Kuzey," said Ela nervously. "Can you carry all of us? You've only been flying for one day."
"I don't have to carry you," I said. "The wind does. I just have to ask."
I closed my eyes and spread my arms. I let go of the ground. And I asked.
"Wind of the east," I said. "Please. Will you carry us to Fūjin? All of us?"
For a moment, nothing.

Then a warm, rushing gust rose up the cliff from the clouds below. It was filled with the smell of pine trees and the sea and something else, something golden, like sunrise. And it lifted all five of us off the platform like leaves.
And Shiro too. She didn't need lifting. She ran beside us *on the air,* her three tails streaming behind her like white flames.
We flew.

Not like a plane, inside a box. Like birds. The wind held us gently, like giant hands, and carried us out over the sea of clouds. The sun was behind us, going down, turning the clouds pink and gold and orange. Ela was screaming, then laughing, then screaming and laughing at the same time. Uncle Tarık held his glasses on with both hands, his eyes squeezed shut, saying something about "the limits of science." Bora flapped his arms as if that would help, shouting "I'M A BIRD! I'M A BIRD! KRUMMI, LOOK AT ME, I'M A BIRD!"
Vera flew beside me. Her hair was streaming back, her eyes huge. She wasn't screaming. She was crying. But she was smiling.
"I never knew," she shouted over the wind. "My father always said wind was a weapon! A tool! He never said it could be *this!*"
"Maybe he never asked it nicely," I shouted back.

The clouds below us were like a white country. Hills and valleys and mountains, all made of cloud, glowing in the sunset. Sometimes a hole opened in them, and through the hole we could see the ground far, far below: green fields, tiny houses, a silver river, a road with little cars on it, like toys.
Then the hole closed, and there was only white again.
And ahead of us, Mount Fuji grew bigger. And bigger. And bigger. Until it filled the whole sky.

The wind carried us up its snowy slope, past black rocks and blue ice, in the last golden light of the sunset. Up and up. Colder and colder. The air got thin. My breath came out in clouds of frost, which the North Wind thought was very nice.
And then we were at the very top.

The top of Mount Fuji is a crater. A huge, round, empty bowl, about as wide as a football stadium, with steep sides, all covered in snow. Around the rim, there are rocks, and a few little wooden buildings, closed for the winter, and a small red shrine at the edge.
The wind set us down softly in the snow, on the rim of the crater.
And standing at the edge of the crater, waiting for us, was a god.

He was twice as tall as a man. His skin was green. Bright, grass green. He had wild white hair that streamed sideways in a wind that wasn't blowing, and a grin full of sharp teeth, and big round eyes that bulged out and shone like lamps. He was wearing nothing but a sort of cloth wrapped around his waist, and a long scarf that floated in the air around him like a ribbon in water.
And on his shoulders was a bag.

A huge white cloth bag, slung over both shoulders, puffing and bulging and wriggling, as if something inside it was alive. Every few seconds, a little gust of wind escaped from the top of it, and he grabbed the opening and pulled it closed again.

Behind him, sitting cross-legged in the snow, was another god. This one had red skin, bright red, as red as Sōjōbō's face. He had horns. Two small ones, on his forehead. And around his body, in a ring, like a giant necklace, was a circle of drums. Big round drums, tied together with rope. He held two drumsticks in his hands.
"So," said Fūjin, the god of wind.
His voice was a hurricane. It blew our hair back. It blew Uncle Tarık's glasses off his nose. Bora caught them.
"This is the little Windborn who asks instead of commanding. Who flies like a baby chicken. Nermin's grandson."
"You know my grandmother?" I said.

"Know her?" Fūjin threw back his head and laughed, and a gust of wind nearly knocked us over. Shiro had to dig all four paws into the snow. "She beat me at cards in 1983! The same year she gave her gate to the foxes! She cheated! I know she cheated! I have never been able to prove it! I still have not forgiven her!"
He looked at me with his bulging eyes. His grin faded.

"But she is in trouble now," he said. "The cold man has her. I can feel it. Every wind in the world can feel it. And the cold man is coming here." He looked toward the north. "Today. He is very close. He walks the fog."
Behind him, his brother Raijin slowly raised his drumsticks.
"So we must be quick," said Fūjin. "I will test you, little Windborn. Pass, and the wind of the sunrise is yours."
"And if I fail?"
Raijin brought his drumsticks down on the biggest drum.
*BOOM.*
The whole sky turned black.
Out of nowhere, a storm came.

Not a normal storm. A *typhoon.* It came spinning out of the dark sky over the sea to the south, black and gigantic, the biggest storm I had ever seen. Bigger than the Poyraz storm on the day Grandma disappeared. Bigger than anything. A huge spinning wheel of black cloud, hundreds of kilometers wide, with lightning flashing inside it like a hundred angry eyes. Its edges were ragged and white, like teeth. And it was turning, slowly, like a great black wheel, and moving.
Moving toward the coast of Japan.
Toward the cities. Where millions of people lived.
"This is my test," said Fūjin. Quietly, now. "Stop it."
"*Stop* it?" I stared at him. "It's a typhoon! It's bigger than a country!"

"Your great-great-grandfather, Kaptan Murat, stopped one in 1856," said Fūjin. "Off the coast of the Black Sea. In a boat with no engine. I was there. I watched." He crouched down, so that his huge green face was level with mine. "The cold man would stop it by freezing it. By smashing it. By *commanding* it. Like you would command a dog to sit. And that would only make it angrier. It would break apart, into a hundred smaller storms, and each one would be worse than the last. They would rage for a month."
He tilted his head.
"How would *you* stop it, little Windborn?"
Raijin beat his drum again. *BOOM.*

Lightning hit the mountain below us. The whole crater shook. Snow slid down the slopes in little avalanches. Uncle Tarık grabbed Ela and held her tight. Bora grabbed Shiro, and hugged her, and she allowed it. Vera stood very still, her hair whipping in the wind, staring at the typhoon.
I looked at the storm.
It was so big. So black. So angry. The lightning flashing. The wind screaming.
I didn't know what to do. I didn't have any idea at all. Freeze it? I couldn't freeze something that big. Blow it away? There wasn't a wind in the world big enough. Fight it? It would eat me alive.
So I did what I always do, when I don't know what to do.
I listened.
I closed my eyes. I let go of the ground, the way Sōjōbō had taught me. I let go of my fear.
And I listened to the typhoon.
At first, all I could hear was the roar. The screaming of the wind. The crash of the thunder. It was so loud. So huge. Like standing next to a jet engine.
But under the roar, there was something else.
Not anger.
*Fear.*
The typhoon was afraid.

It was a huge, young, frightened wind. Born only a few days ago, out over the warm ocean, far to the south. It had started small, just a little spinning breeze. And then it had started to grow. And spin faster. And grow more. And spin faster. Bigger and bigger and faster and faster. And it didn't know how to stop. It didn't know what was happening to it. It was spinning so fast that it was dizzy, and frightened, and it was screaming because it was frightened, and the screaming made it spin faster.
Like a little kid on a merry-go-round, screaming because it's going too fast, and nobody will make it stop.
"It's scared," I said slowly. I opened my eyes. "It's not angry. It's scared. It doesn't want to hurt anyone. It just doesn't know how to stop."
Fūjin's bulging eyes glittered.
I took a deep breath.
And I let all three winds inside me out at once. Not as a blast. Not as a weapon. As a *voice.*
The North Wind. The Black Wind. The Keşişleme. Singing together.

I don't know what song it was. It wasn't a song I knew. It didn't have any words. It was slow, and soft, and calm. Like the song Grandma used to sing to me when I couldn't sleep. That old Black Sea song, about the fisherman, and the girl waiting on the shore. Not those words. Not that tune. But the feeling of it. The feeling of being sung to. In the dark. By someone who loves you.

The North Wind sang it cool and clear. The Black Wind sang it low and deep. The Keşişleme sang it warm. And I sang it too, with my real voice, out loud, on the top of Mount Fuji, in the wind and the snow, not caring how stupid I sounded.
The song went out across the sea. A slow, warm sound. It went out across the dark water, toward the spinning black storm. And it wrapped around the typhoon like a blanket.
*Slow down,* the song said. *You're safe. You're not alone. Someone's here. Slow down. Slow down.*
The typhoon wobbled.
Its spinning slowed. Just a little.
I kept singing.

It slowed again. Then more. The lightning flickered. Faded. The screaming of the wind got quieter. Quieter. The black clouds began to turn gray. The ragged edges softened. The great wheel turned slower, and slower, and slower, like a merry-go-round at the end of the day.
And then it stopped.

The typhoon fell apart. Gently. The gray clouds turned white, and drifted apart, and broke up into a hundred soft rain clouds, scattered across the sea. And they rained. Soft, gentle rain, falling on an empty ocean, far from any land. Like crying, after you've been very scared, when you're finally safe.
The sun came out. Low and gold, on the horizon, in the last of the sunset.
I stopped singing.
I fell to my knees in the snow, completely exhausted. My whole body was shaking. My throat was raw. I couldn't feel my fingers.
Fūjin was laughing again. A big, booming, happy laugh, that blew the snow off the rim of the crater. He picked me up with one enormous green hand and set me on my feet.

"Nine hundred years," he said. "Nine hundred years I have been testing them. Kings and priests and warriors and wizards. And only three Windborn have ever passed that test. Your great-great-grandfather, Kaptan Murat. The girl from Persia with the red scarf. And now you." His bulging eyes were shining. "And not one of them did it with a *song.*"
Raijin, behind him, put down his drumsticks. He was smiling too.

Fūjin reached into his great white bag. He rummaged around in it for a while, with his arm in up to the shoulder, while little gusts of wind escaped and swirled around us. Then he pulled out a bronze needle.
It glowed red-gold. Like the morning sun. Like the first light of sunrise on the snow.
"The Gündoğusu," he said. "The wind of the sunrise. The east wind. It is yours, little Windborn."
He held it out.
And a gray hand reached past me and took it.
He was standing right behind me. I hadn't heard him come. Nobody had. Not even the winds.
Mordecai Vane.

In his long gray coat, holding the Gündoğusu Key in his gray stone hand. Behind him, the fog was rolling up over the rim of the crater, thick and gray and cold, from nowhere, from the fog road. And Vex was stepping out of it, his face pale, his gray gloves on.

Up close, Mordecai looked older than he had in Grandma's kitchen. Much older. His face was thin and tired, with deep lines around his mouth. His dark hair had more gray in it. And his stone hand was terrible. It was gray all the way up past his wrist now, and covered in cracks, like a dry riverbed. Little pieces of stone flaked off it when he moved his fingers, and drifted away on the wind like ash.
In the stone hand, two Keys. The Lodos, cold and dull and gray, like an old spoon. And the Gündoğusu, still glowing red-gold, but flickering now. Frost spreading across it. Fading.
It was screaming. I could hear it. A thin, high scream, getting quieter.
But his eyes were the same cold green as his children's. And his smile still had too many teeth.

"Thank you, Fūjin," he said. "And thank you, Kuzey. I could never have passed that test myself. I would have frozen the typhoon, and it would have ruined everything." He tucked the Key into his coat. "You did the hard work. I just collected. As usual."
"Give it back," I said. My voice cracked. My whole body was still shaking from the song. I could barely stand up.
Fūjin roared.

It was the loudest sound I have ever heard. Louder than Tepegöz. Louder than the Troll Queen. Louder than the typhoon. He swung his great white bag at Mordecai like a club, and a hurricane came out of it, a howling wall of wind that could have knocked down a building.
Mordecai raised his stone hand.
And a wall of ice burst up out of the snow between them. Thick as a castle wall. Blue and white and glittering. The hurricane hit it, and howled, and couldn't get through.
Raijin's drums thundered. *BOOM. BOOM. BOOM.* Lightning struck the ice wall. Three times. Four. It cracked. It didn't break.
"Please," said Mordecai, behind his wall. Calmly. Politely. Like a man at a dinner party. "I'm not here to fight gods. I have what I came for. I'm leaving."
"How did you find us?" Ela shouted.
Mordecai's cold green eyes turned slowly toward her.
Then toward Vera.
"Ask my daughter," he said.
Vera went white.
As white as the snow. As white as Shiro.
"I didn't tell you anything!" she said. Her voice was shaking. "I didn't! I never told you anything! I never called you, I never..."
"No," said Mordecai gently. "You didn't. You were very good. Very careful. I was proud of you, in a way." He pointed with one gray finger. "But your mother's bracelet did."
Everyone looked at Vera's wrist.
At the thin silver bracelet. At the little gray stone.

"I put a tracker in that stone," said Mordecai, "the week after your mother died. A very small one. Very clever. It runs on the cold. It will run forever. So that I would always know where you were. Wherever you went." He smiled. "I am your father, Vera. I worry about you."
Vera stared at the bracelet.
She didn't say *I didn't know.* She didn't say *that's not true.*

Because she *had* known. I saw it in her face. She had known since Iceland. She had heard it clicking on the stairs of the gray tower. She had sat on the steps of the temple at Kurama, with her thumbnail against the stone, trying to take it out.
*Not yet. I can't. Not yet.*
She hadn't been able to. Because it was her mother's.
Her face crumpled.
"How do you even *get* here?" said Bora. He was standing in front of Ela, with his arms out, like a wall. His voice was shaking, but he said it anyway. "We had to *fly!* On the *wind!*"
Mordecai looked at him. He almost seemed amused.

"I didn't fly," he said. "I can't. The wind will not carry me. It never has." He took off his gray glove. The cracks in his stone hand were even worse underneath it. Cold mist poured out of them. "Forty years ago, Bora, I was Nermin Aydın's best student. Did they tell you that? I wanted to be a Windborn more than anything in the world. I studied for years. I learned every language the winds had ever spoken. And they never spoke to me. Not once. Never."
His face twisted.
"So I found another way. An old way. The fog roads. The gray hand. The gray hand doesn't ask the wind." He clenched his stone fist. "It *takes.*"
And all around us, the wind on the mountain stopped.
Just stopped. Dead. Like someone had turned off a fan.

The snow that had been blowing in the air hung there, frozen, in midair, all around us, like a photograph. Fūjin's white hair stopped streaming. His floating scarf fell. Raijin's drums went silent. The little gusts that kept escaping from Fūjin's bag stopped, and the bag sagged, like a balloon going down.
I tried to call the winds inside me. They were there. I could feel them. But they felt far away. Muffled. Like voices under water. Like shouting in a dream.

"Two to three," said Mordecai softly. He was looking at me. "Soon, it will be seven to none." He pulled his glove back on, slowly. "Your grandmother is waiting for you, Kuzey. Not in the tower. Not anymore. I have moved her. To the Gate. Bring me your Keys, and she goes home. Don't, and she stays in the cold. Forever."
He turned. He looked at Vex.
"Come," he said.
Vex looked at his sister. Just for a second. She was standing in the frozen snow, holding her wrist, crying. He opened his mouth.
Then he closed it, and followed his father.
The frozen snow parted around Mordecai Vane like a curtain. He walked into the fog, and the fog swallowed him, and his son, and they were gone.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Six: Get the Bad Thing Out
p: When he was gone, the wind came back all at once.

Howling. Furious. The snow that had been hanging frozen in the air came crashing down all at once, like someone had dropped a bucket. Fūjin's hair streamed out sideways again. His bag puffed up. He threw back his head and roared at the sky, so loud that the snow slid off the rim of the crater in a great white avalanche, all the way down into the bowl. Raijin was beating his drums so hard that thunder rolled across the whole of Japan. People in Tokyo heard it, I found out later. It was on the news.
Vera sat down in the snow.
She just sat. Right where she was standing. As if her legs had stopped working. She was staring at her bracelet, holding her wrist with her other hand.

"It was my mother's," she said, in a small voice. To nobody. To the snow. "She gave it to me when I was six. Right before she died. It's the only thing I have from her. The only thing in the whole world."
She looked up at me, and her eyes were full of tears.

"I knew," she said. "Since Iceland. I heard it clicking. On the stairs. I wasn't sure. I didn't *want* to be sure. And I couldn't... I tried to take it off, Kuzey. At the temple. I tried. And I couldn't. Because it was hers."
She was crying so hard now that she could barely speak.
"It's my fault. He found you because of me. Every time. The Grays, at the airport in Cairo. The hotel. The museum. Everywhere. It was me. It was always me. He took the Key because of me."
