"No," I said. I sat down in the snow next to her. "No. It's his fault. Not yours. He did it. Not you."
"I should have told you."

"Maybe," I said. "But you were scared. And it was your mom's." I thought about Grandma's blue scarf, which I had been wearing every single day since Istanbul. I hadn't taken it off once. Not even to sleep. "I would have been scared too."
Ela knelt down in front of her.
Ela. Who never trusted anyone. Who had been at sixty percent in Iceland, and eighty-five in Egypt, and ninety-five in Cairo, in a room with a ceiling fan, talking in the dark.
She held out her hand.
"Give it to me," she said quietly. "I'll take the stone out. You can keep the bracelet. The stone was his. Not your mom's. The bracelet was hers. Get the bad thing out, and keep the rest."
Vera stared at her.
Then she looked at me. I remembered the temple steps. *Get the bad thing out. And keep the rest.*
Vera hesitated for a long time. Her hand was shaking.
Then she took off the bracelet, and gave it to Ela.

Ela took a tiny screwdriver from her pocket. (She always carries one. Don't ask. A detective has to be ready for anything.) She held the bracelet very carefully in the palm of her hand. She bent over it, with her glasses pushed down on her nose, and her tongue sticking out of the corner of her mouth, the way it does when she's concentrating very hard.
Very, very carefully, she pried out the little gray stone.
It came out with a tiny *click.*
Underneath it, in the silver setting, there was a little chip. Black. As small as a grain of rice. With a tiny red light on it, blinking.
*Blink. Blink. Blink.*
Ela held it up on the tip of the screwdriver. Nobody said anything.
Then she gave it to Vera.

Vera took it. She looked at it for a long, long moment. The tiny blinking light. The thing her father had put inside her mother's present, a week after the funeral. So he would always know where she was.
Then she stood up.
She walked to the edge of the great crater of Mount Fuji. She stood there in the wind, with her hair blowing, looking down into the huge white bowl of snow.
And she threw it as far as she could.
It flew out over the crater, a tiny black speck, and disappeared into the snow.
Gone.
Ela came up beside her and gave her back the bracelet. It was just a thin silver chain now, with an empty little setting where the stone had been.
Vera put it on. She held it against her chest, with both hands, and closed her eyes.
"Thank you," she whispered.
Bora sat down next to her in the snow and took something out of his pocket. A rice ball, wrapped in seaweed, a bit squashed. He had been saving it since the morning.
"Emergency," he explained, and handed it to her.
Vera laughed through her tears, and ate it.
That was when the little breeze arrived.

It came across the crater, very faint, very tired. A thin, small, ordinary breeze. It had come from a long way away. From the north, across the sea. It had been traveling for days and days, from a cold gray tower in the fog, over Scotland and Norway and Russia and Siberia and the whole of Asia. Getting smaller and weaker every day. Almost gone.
It found me. It brushed against my cheek, so softly that I almost didn't notice it.
And it whispered, in a voice I knew better than any voice in the world. Crackly. Old. Very faint.
*Tell him. Tell my Kuzey. The girl. The girl's bracelet. Tell him to look at the girl's bracelet.*
Then it was gone. Used up. Finished.
I sat there in the snow. Ela was looking at me. So was Vera.
"Kuzey?" said Ela. "What is it?"
"Grandma," I said slowly. "She sent a message. On the wind. A long time ago, I think. Days ago." I swallowed. "She said to look at Vera's bracelet."
There was a long silence.
Then Bora started to laugh. He couldn't help it. It just came out of him, the way it always does.
"Too late, Grandma," he said, wiping his eyes. "Too late. We already did it."

And then we were all laughing, even Vera, on the top of Mount Fuji, in the snow and the wind. Laughing so hard that it hurt. Because it was terrible, and it was funny, and we had lost the Key, and Grandma was so far away. But she was trying to help. She was always trying to help.
"Kuzey," said Ela, when she could breathe again. "Your grandmother tried to warn us. From a prison. In a tower. Through the *wind.*"
"She's very stubborn," I said.
"I like her already," said Vera.

Fūjin was still angry when we came over to the shrine. Very angry. The wind around his head whipped his white hair in circles. Every few seconds, a small tornado spun off him and knocked over a stone lantern.
"He stole from ME," he roared. "From MY BAG! In MY HOUSE! On MY MOUNTAIN!"
"I'm sorry," I said. "I failed. You gave me the Key and I let him take it."
Fūjin stopped.
He looked down at me with his bulging eyes. Slowly, the little tornadoes around his head calmed down. His hair stopped whipping and drifted.
"Failed?" he said.
He crouched down, in the snow, his huge green face close to mine.

"Little Windborn. You passed my test. You calmed a typhoon with a song. A *song.* No one has ever done that. The Key was a prize. A reward." He poked me in the chest with one enormous green finger. "*You* are the treasure. Not the Key."
I didn't know what to say.

"And I will tell you a secret about the gray hand," said Fūjin, lowering his hurricane voice to a whisper, which was still quite loud. "It can take a wind. It can hold a wind. It can squeeze a wind until it obeys. But it cannot make a wind *love* it. Every wind it takes is fighting it. Every second. Every day. That is why his hand is cracked. Did you see? That is why he is so tired. That is why he looks so old."
I thought about the Lodos, whispering to me from Vex's pocket in Crete. *I will come back to you. Wait for me.* I thought about the Gündoğusu, screaming in his fist, fading.
"The Keys he has," I said slowly. "They're trying to come back to me."
"Yes." Fūjin grinned his sharp grin. "And when the Gate opens, and all seven winds are together in one place, every one of them will remember. Who asked." He tapped my chest. "And who took."
He stood up. He reached into his great bag once more, and rummaged around for a long time, muttering.
"Now," he said. "A gift. Because Nermin beat me at cards, and I am a good loser. Mostly. Sometimes."
He pulled out a small white cloth bag. No bigger than my hand. Tied with a red cord.

"A wind bag," he said. "Like mine. Very small. It holds one breath of the east wind. The fastest wind in the world. When you need to be somewhere fast, very fast, faster than flying, open it. But only once. One breath. Then it is gone."
I took it carefully. It wriggled in my hand like a hamster.
"And this," said Raijin.

It was the first time he had spoken. His voice was deep and rumbling, like thunder far away. He held out his hand to Bora. In it was a tiny drum. Small enough to hang on a necklace, on a red cord. Round and red, with a tiny drumstick tied to it.
"For the Beastspeaker," said Raijin. "When animals are needed, beat it once. Only once. They will hear it across a thousand miles. And they will come."
Bora held the little drum like it was made of glass. "Thank you," he said. He bowed very low, the way Shiro had taught him on the way up the mountain. "Thank you very much, Mr. Raijin."
Raijin nodded his horned head. Then, very slowly, he smiled.
"The fox told me about the Minotaur," he said. "And the baklava." His smile grew. "Next time, bring me some."
The wind carried us back down the mountain in the dark, under the stars.

Not to Kyoto. Shiro said she knew a place. A little town at the foot of Mount Fuji, by a lake, with an old inn with hot springs. The wind put us down softly at the edge of the lake, by the light of the moon. Mount Fuji rose above us, black against the stars, with its snowy top glowing faintly.
And upside down in the still water of the lake was its reflection. A perfect, upside-down mountain, made of stars.
Shiro sat on a rock at the edge of the water. Her three tails were wrapped around her feet. She looked at us for a long time with her gold eyes.
Then she spoke to Bora.
Bora listened. His face went sad.

"She says she has to go home," he said. "To Fushimi Inari. To her gates. She says the foxes need her. She says the god Inari will be cross that she's been away so long." He listened again. "She says she's going to get her fourth tail in sixty-three years, and she has to practice."
"Practice what?" said Ela.
"Being magnificent," said Bora.

Shiro jumped down off the rock. She walked to each of us in turn. She sniffed Uncle Tarık's shoes, and sneezed. She looked at Ela for a long time, and swished her tails, which Bora said meant *clever.* She went to Vera and pushed her nose against Vera's hand, the one with the empty bracelet on it, very gently.
She came to me. She looked up at me with her gold eyes.
Bora translated.
"She says," he said, "'Tell your grandmother the gate is still standing. Tell her the foxes have kept it clean for her. Tell her to come and visit.'"
"I will," I said.
Then she went to Bora.

She sat in front of him, and looked up at him, and for a long time neither of them said anything at all. Then Bora knelt down, and Shiro put her front paws on his knees, and pushed her pointed white face into his neck.
When she pulled back, there was something in his hand.
A single white hair. Long and silver-white. From one of her tails.
"She says," said Bora, and his voice wobbled, "if I'm ever lost, hold it up, and a fox will find me. Anywhere in the world." He looked at the hair. "She says it's from her third tail. Her favorite."
He put it in his hat, next to Krummi's feather.

Shiro swished her three tails one last time. Then she turned and ran. Not along the ground. Up. Into the air. Running on the moonlight, across the lake, her three tails streaming behind her like white flames, up and up into the starry sky, getting smaller and smaller, until she was just a white spark among the stars.
Then she was gone.
Bora stood at the edge of the lake for a long time, looking at the sky.
"I'm going to have to get a bigger hat," he said.

chapters.t: Chapter Thirty: Meanwhile, Leaving the Gray Tower
p: *Kuzey heard about this much later. From Grandma Nermin herself.*

Two days before Mount Fuji, Mordecai Vane had come up the stairs of the gray tower at midnight, and unlocked the door of the little cold room at the top, and said, "Get your coat, Nermin. We're leaving."
Grandma had looked up from her chair by the window, where she was knitting a scarf from wool that Vera had smuggled up to her, weeks ago.
"Where are we going?" she said.
"Home," said Mordecai. "Or near enough. Turkey. Cappadocia." He smiled his thin smile. "To the Gate."
Grandma put down her knitting very slowly.
"You don't have the Keys," she said. "You have one. My grandson has three."

"I'll have two by tomorrow," said Mordecai. "And the boy will bring me the rest. He'll have to. Because you'll be waiting for him at the Gate." He held out his human hand, his left one. "Your coat, Nermin."
She looked at him for a long time. Then she stood up and put on her coat. And she put the half-knitted scarf in her pocket.

The fog road was cold. Colder than anything. They walked through the gray for what felt like hours. Grandma held her coat tight around her, and hummed the old Black Sea song to keep warm, and Mordecai walked in front of her and did not tell her to stop.
When the fog cleared, they were underground.

In a tunnel. Cut out of soft pink stone. With low ceilings and narrow passages and stairs going down, and down, and down, into the earth. Little rooms carved out of the rock on either side, empty, with holes in the walls for lamps. Round stone doors, like giant millstones, standing by the openings, ready to be rolled across.
"Derinkuyu," said Grandma softly. "The city beneath the city. I haven't been here for forty years."

"Eighteen floors," said Mordecai. "Eighty-five meters deep. People hid here from wars, for thousands of years. Thousands of people. With their animals and their food and their children. For months at a time." He walked on, down the stairs. "And at the very bottom, under everything, the old builders found something. Something that was already there before they came. Something they didn't understand. So they built their city on top of it, and hid it, and forgot it."

They went down. And down. And down. Floor after floor. Past stables and kitchens and wells and wine cellars, and a little church with a cross carved in the wall. Past air shafts going straight up, so deep that you couldn't see the top.
At the bottom of the last staircase, there was a door.
A door of rock. With seven sides. And seven holes.
And a warm light coming through the cracks around it. Seven colors, shifting and turning, like a rainbow trapped in the stone.
The Gate of Seven Winds.
Grandma stood in front of it for a long time. Her face was very still. Mordecai watched her.
"You knew it was here," he said. "All along. You've always known."
"Every Keeper knows," said Grandma. "We're told when we're young. And we never, ever come here. Never. Not unless the world is ending." She looked at him. "Is the world ending, Mordecai?"
He didn't answer.
He showed her where she would stay. A little room carved into the rock, beside the Gate. A bed. A chair. A table. A lamp. A small stove. And, on the table, a teapot and two glasses.
Grandma looked at the teapot.
Then she looked at Mordecai.
"You brought a teapot," she said.
He didn't look at her. "You always said a room without boiling tea is just a room with a chair in it."
"A kitchen," said Grandma. "I said a *kitchen.* With a *fridge.*"
"Close enough," said Mordecai. And he turned and walked away, fast, up the stairs, before she could see his face.
Grandma Nermin sat down in the chair, in the little stone room at the bottom of the world, next to the Gate of Seven Winds. She looked at the teapot for a long time.
Then she took out her knitting and started again.

chapters.t: Chapter Thirty-One: Meanwhile, at the Bottom of the Fog
p: *And this part Kuzey heard from Vex.*
When they came out of the fog road at Derinkuyu, with the Gündoğusu in his father's fist, Vex took the little black screen out of his pocket.
The map of Japan.
No red dot.
Nothing. Just the map. The mountains and the cities and the sea. Empty.
He stared at it for a long time.
"It's gone," he said. "The dot. Vera's dot. It's gone."

His father didn't even look. "The fox girl's friend found it," he said. "The clever one, with the glasses. I thought she would, eventually. It doesn't matter now." He held up his stone hand, with the two Keys in it, the cold gray Lodos and the fading red-gold Gündoğusu. "I don't need to follow them anymore. They'll come to me. They have to. I have the one thing the boy wants more than any Key."
He walked away down the stairs, toward the Gate, toward Grandma's room.
Vex stood alone in the tunnel. Looking at the empty screen.
And he felt something he didn't understand. Something warm, in his chest. Something that loosened, just a little, like a knot coming undone.
*She's free,* he thought. *He can't find her anymore. She's free.*
He switched off the screen. He put it in his pocket.
And then, alone in the dark at the bottom of the underground city, where his father couldn't see, Vex Vane smiled.
It wasn't his father's smile. It didn't have too many teeth. It was small, and a bit wobbly, and nobody saw it at all.
The inn by the lake had an onsen. A hot spring. Outdoors.

It was a big round pool made of smooth black rocks, steaming in the cold night air, with a little wooden roof over one end and lanterns hanging from it. The water came up from deep under Mount Fuji, Uncle Tarık said, heated by the volcano. It smelled a little of minerals. Snow lay on the rocks around the edge. And above it, filling the whole sky, was the mountain.

The boys' pool and the girls' pool were separated by a tall bamboo fence. Uncle Tarık and Bora and I sat in the boys' side, up to our chins in the hot water, looking at the mountain in the moonlight. Through the fence, we could hear Ela and Vera, talking quietly. Sometimes laughing.
It was the first time Vera had laughed since the crater.
"Uncle Tarık," I said. "I failed. Again. Like Crete."

Uncle Tarık didn't say anything for a while. He was looking up at Mount Fuji. The steam from the water had fogged up his glasses completely, so he had taken them off. Without them, he looked younger. And very tired.
"You calmed a typhoon," he said. "With a song. You saved... Kuzey, I don't know how many people. Thousands? Millions? That storm was heading for the coast."
"But Mordecai got the Key."
"Yes," said Uncle Tarık. "He did. That's two to three now. Not three to one anymore." He sighed. "But you know what I keep thinking about?"
"What?"

"He said, *you did the hard work. I just collected.*" Uncle Tarık sank down a little further into the water. "He's done that every time. In Crete. Now here. He can't find the Keys. He can't pass the tests. He can't answer the riddles, or make friends with the Minotaur, or sing to a typhoon. All he can do is wait until someone else does the hard part, and then take it." He shook his head. "That's not strength, Kuzey. That's the opposite. That's a man who can't do anything himself."
Bora, who had been floating on his back with his eyes closed, opened one eye.
"Like the kid in school," he said, "who copies your homework. And then gets a better mark than you. Because his handwriting is neater."
"Exactly like that," said Uncle Tarık.
"I hate that kid," said Bora, and closed his eye again.
Through the fence, I heard Vera's voice. Quiet. Talking to Ela.

"My mother had a rule," she was saying. "When we were small. If you lose something, it's not your fault. If you lose something because you were careless, it's your fault, but you can fix it. And if somebody takes something from you, it's never, ever your fault. Not ever. It's theirs."
"That's a good rule," said Ela.
"I forgot it," said Vera. "For a long time. I just remembered it. In the crater."
There was a long pause.
"I'm going to write it in the Clue Book," said Ela. "On the first page. Under Grandma's."
Later, when everyone else had gone inside, I stayed in the hot water alone.

The moon had moved across the sky. Mount Fuji glowed white above me. The steam rose and drifted. It was very quiet. Just the trickle of hot water coming into the pool, and an owl, somewhere, far away.
"Gündoğusu," I said, very quietly. "Wind of the sunrise. Can you hear me?"
Nothing.
"I'm sorry," I said. "I'm sorry he took you. I'm going to get you back. I promise. I'll get you and the Lodos back. And then you'll be free. All of you."
For a long time, nothing at all.
Then, very faint, so faint that it might have been the steam, or the owl, or my own imagination, a tiny warm breath touched my face. From very far away. From the west. From under the ground.
It smelled like sunrise.
*I know,* it whispered. *We know. We are waiting.*

chapters.t: Chapter Thirty-Three: A Letter to the Ice
p: On our last night in Japan, I wrote a letter to my parents.
Not an email. Not a message. A real letter, on paper. Ela tore a page out of the back of the Clue Book for me, which she has never done for anyone, ever, and lent me her best pencil.
I wasn't going to send it. Not yet. I was going to keep it, and give it to them when they came home from the ice. When Grandma was home too. When it was over.
I sat on the floor of our room at the inn, by the window, with Mount Fuji glowing white in the moonlight outside, and I wrote.
*Dear Mom and Dad,*
*You're going to read this when you get home. I hope Grandma is sitting next to you when you read it. If she is, she will probably be making tea. Say hi to her for me. Even though I'll be there too.*

*There are some things I didn't tell you on our Sunday calls. I'm sorry. I didn't want you to worry, because you were at the bottom of the world and you couldn't do anything. But now you're home, so I can tell you.*
*Grandma didn't go to visit her friends. She was kidnapped. By a man with a hand made of stone. I know that sounds crazy. It's true.*

*Also, I can talk to the wind. I always could, a little bit. Now I can a lot. I have three winds living inside me. They're called the Yıldız and the Karayel and the Keşişleme. When I breathe out, sometimes it snows. Sometimes a tiny black cloud comes out. Sometimes sand. Uncle Tarık says it's very unhygienic.*
*I can fly now. A tengu taught me. A tengu is a Japanese mountain spirit with a very long nose. He said I need to practice for a hundred years.*

*Bora can talk to animals. He has made friends with a Minotaur, a raven, a horse, a camel, about fifty cats, some seals, some deer and a fox with three tails. He has a feather and a fox hair in his hat. He says he needs a bigger hat.*
*Ela solved about a hundred puzzles. She's the smartest person I've ever met. Don't tell her I said that.*
*Uncle Tarık used all his airline miles. He was very brave. He fought six men with an umbrella. He flew a kite.*

*There's a girl called Vera. Her dad is the man with the stone hand. But she's on our side. Her mom died when she was six. She wants to be a marine biologist, like you. I think you'd like her. Could she come and visit? She doesn't really have anywhere to go.*
*I sang to a typhoon. It stopped.*
*I miss you every day. I miss the frozen video calls. I even miss the penguin stories. Is it the same penguin? Dad says it is. I believe him.*
*I'm scared sometimes. Most of the time, actually. But my friends are here, and the winds are here, and Grandma is waiting for me, and I'm going to bring her home.*
*I love you to the North Star and back.*
*Kuzey*
*P.S. I've been wearing a scarf. Grandma's blue one. Every day. You can tell her.*
I folded it up very small. I put it in the inside pocket of my coat, next to Grandma's letter from the Serpent Column, which had gone so soft from reading that it was like a piece of cloth.
Vera was sitting on her futon on the other side of the room, watching me. She had been watching the whole time.
"Who's it to?" she said.
"My mom and dad," I said. "For when they come home."
She was quiet for a while.
"Did you tell them about me?" she said.
"Yes."
"What did you say?"
"I said you were on our side," I said. "And that you want to be a marine biologist. And I asked if you could come and visit."
Vera looked at me for a long time. Her face did something complicated.
Then she lay down on her futon, and pulled the quilt up to her chin, and turned to face the wall.
"Goodnight, Kuzey," she said. Her voice sounded thick.
"Goodnight, Vera."
Outside, the moonlight shone on Mount Fuji. Inside my coat, the two letters lay together, one old and soft, one new and crisp.
And for the first time in a long time, I fell asleep straight away.

chapters.t: Chapter Thirty-Four: The Voice in the East Wind
p: The next morning, we stood at the edge of the lake, watching the sun rise behind Mount Fuji.

It came up slowly. First the sky went pale. Then pink. Then gold. Then a single point of fire appeared, right at the very top of the mountain, right in the middle of the crater. For a moment, it looked like Mount Fuji was holding the sun on its peak, like a candle. A diamond. The lake reflected it, upside down. Two mountains. Two suns.
"Diamond Fuji," whispered Vera. "That's what they call it. When the sun rises right on top. It only happens a few days a year. People wait for hours to see it."
Ela had the Clue Book open. She was writing the score.
*Kuzey: 3 (Yıldız, Karayel, Keşişleme)*
*Mordecai: 2 (Lodos, Gündoğusu)*
*Keys left: 2 (Poyraz, Kıble)*
*New friends: Shiro, Sōjōbō, Karasu, Fūjin, Raijin, the Okami-san, the man at the sushi restaurant*
*Bad things removed: 1 tracker*
"Two left," she said. "Poyraz and Kıble. The northeast and the south."
"And the Gate," said Uncle Tarık quietly.
I took out the leather map and unrolled it on a rock by the water.
Five stars were dark now. Istanbul. Crete. Iceland. Egypt. Japan.
Two were still glowing.
One far across the Pacific Ocean, on the other side of the world, in the jungles of Mexico. Green and gold, like feathers.
And one, brighter than all the others, in the very center of Turkey.
Cappadocia.
It was pulsing. Brighter. Dimmer. Brighter. Dimmer. Faster than before. Like a heartbeat that was speeding up.
"He said the Gate," I said. "He said Grandma is waiting at the Gate. He moved her there."
"Then we go to Cappadocia," said Bora. "Right now. Today."
"No," said Vera suddenly.
Everyone looked at her.
She was standing very straight, with her hand on her empty bracelet. Her face was pale, but her voice was steady.

"If we go to the Gate now, with only three Keys," she said, "he'll take them from you. He'll freeze Uncle Tarık, or Ela, or Bora, like he always does, and you'll give them to him, because you always do. Because you're *you.* And then he'll have five. And he'll only need the last two. And he'll find them himself. Or he'll make someone else find them, and then take them." She took a deep breath. "My father always has a plan. Always. He'll be ready for us."
"So what do we do?" said Ela.

"We get to Mexico first," said Vera. "We have to find the Poyraz before he does. Then it's four to two. Then he *needs* you, more than you need him. Then *we* have something to bargain with." She looked at me. "That's what he'd do. If he was us. I know how he thinks. I've watched him think my whole life."
Ela looked at Vera with something new in her eyes. Something I had never seen Ela look at anyone with before. Not even me.
Respect.
"She's right," said Ela.
And at that moment, the east wind blew across the lake.

It came out of the sunrise. Warm and golden. It rippled the water and broke up the reflection of Fuji into a thousand shining pieces. And inside it, so faint that I almost thought I imagined it, I heard a voice. A voice I knew better than any voice in the world.

Not tired, this time. Not a tiny breeze, used up after days of traveling. Strong. Clear. As if it had come on a fast, warm wind. A wind that had been taken. A wind in a stone hand. That had escaped, just for a second, just long enough, to carry one message.
*Kuzey. My Kuzey. I can hear you. Through the winds he stole. The sunrise wind is with me, and it told me everything. The typhoon. The song. Oh, my clever boy. A song.*
My heart stopped.
*I am under the ground. In the city beneath the city. By the Gate. I am all right. Do not come for me yet. Find the serpent of feathers first. The Poyraz. Hurry. He is going to Mexico too.*
"Grandma," I whispered. "Grandma!"
But the wind had already moved on. Out across the lake. Toward the mountain. Toward the rising sun.
I stood there with tears running down my face, and I didn't care who saw.
Then I wiped my eyes, and I rolled up the map, and I turned to the others.
"Mexico," I said.
"Mexico," said everyone together.
And from somewhere high above us, from the very top of Mount Fuji, in the golden light of the sunrise, a voice like a hurricane came rolling down across the lake.
*GO, LITTLE WINDBORN!* roared Fūjin. *AND TELL NERMIN I WANT A REMATCH!*

For hundreds of years, sailors on the Black Sea, the Bosphorus and the Mediterranean used a wind rose to name the winds. Each wind had its own name and its own personality, and every sailor knew them by heart. These are the seven winds of the Order of the Compass Rose.
**Yıldız (North).** Named after the North Star, *yıldız* means "star." A cold, clear, starry wind. Kuzey's own wind.
**Poyraz (Northeast).** The great wind of the Black Sea. When the Poyraz blows hard, the fishermen go home and the ferries rock.
**Gündoğusu (East).** "Sunrise." The wind that comes from where the sun is born each morning.
**Keşişleme (Southeast).** Named after the monks, the *keşiş,* who lived on the mountains to the southeast. A warm, dry wind from the deserts.
**Kıble (South).** The wind from the direction of Mecca. Hot, and full of sand.
**Lodos (Southwest).** A warm, wild, wet wind that brings big waves and headaches. People in Istanbul say the Lodos makes everyone grumpy.
**Karayel (Northwest).** "Black wind." A stormy, dark wind that brings clouds and sudden rain.
And the eighth, the west wind, the **Batı**, the one that would not make a deal? Nobody knows. It is still wild. That is another story.

chapters.t: The Real Places in This Book
p: **The Shinkansen.** Japan's bullet trains really do travel at around 300 kilometers an hour, and on a clear day you can see Mount Fuji from the window between Tokyo and Kyoto.
**Ryokan.** Traditional Japanese inns, with tatami floors, futons, sliding paper doors, and a lot of rules about slippers.

**Fushimi Inari.** A real shrine in Kyoto, with thousands of orange torii gates winding up a mountain, and fox statues everywhere, some with keys in their mouths. The names of the people who donated the gates really are written on them.
**Kitsune.** Fox spirits from Japanese folklore. In the old stories, they really do grow new tails as they get older and wiser. The most powerful have nine.
**Nara's deer.** Real, and there are more than a thousand of them. Many really do bow to people with crackers.
**Mount Kurama.** A real mountain north of Kyoto, with a temple, a forest of huge old cedars and a real Path of Roots. Legend says the tengu king Sōjōbō trained the young warrior Ushiwakamaru there.
**Tengu.** Mountain spirits from Japanese folklore, with wings, and either crow beaks or long noses and red faces.
**Fūjin and Raijin.** The Japanese gods of wind and thunder. Fūjin really is shown carrying a bag of winds on his shoulders, and Raijin really is shown surrounded by drums.
**Mount Fuji.** A real volcano, 3,776 meters high, with a crater at the top. It last erupted in 1707. The painter Hokusai really did make a famous series called *Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.*
**Diamond Fuji.** On a few days each year, from certain places, the sun really does rise or set exactly on the summit, like a diamond on a ring.
*Here is the first chapter of the next book,* The Feathered Serpent.
**Chapter One: Across the Pacific**

From Tokyo to Mexico City is twelve hours on a plane, across the whole Pacific Ocean, the biggest ocean in the world. You fly across a date line, and you arrive before you left. It's the strangest thing. You leave Tokyo on Tuesday evening, and you land in Mexico on Tuesday afternoon. Bora said it meant we got an extra Tuesday for free, and he was going to spend it eating.
We didn't sit next to the toilets this time. Uncle Tarık had finally run out of every kind of airline miles, and Dr. Amira's cousin's tiny airline didn't fly to Mexico. So Vera paid.

"I have money," she said, at the ticket desk in Tokyo, very quietly. She took out a card. A black one. "My father gave me this card when I was ten. For emergencies. He never checks it. He never checks anything I do with money." She looked at the card for a long moment. "I think this is an emergency."
"Vera," said Uncle Tarık. "Are you sure? Won't he know?"
"He'll know," said Vera. "I don't care anymore." She handed the card to the lady at the desk. "Four... no, five tickets to Mexico City, please. Not next to the toilets."

So for the first time in this whole adventure, we sat in proper seats. In the middle of the plane. With a window. And enough legroom that Bora could stretch out his legs, which he did, and kept saying "Look! Look how far my legs go!" until Ela told him to stop.

Vera sat by the window again. She looked out at the ocean for hours. Endless blue, wrinkled like a blanket, sparkling in the sun. Sometimes there were tiny islands, green and white. Sometimes there were ships, so small they looked like grains of rice.
She kept touching her wrist. Where the bracelet was. The empty bracelet, with its little empty silver setting where the gray stone had been.
"Does it feel strange?" I asked her. "Without the stone?"
She thought about it.

"Lighter," she said. "It feels lighter. Like when you take off a backpack you've been carrying all day, and you forgot it was there." She turned the bracelet around on her wrist. "It's still hers. My mom's. It's more hers now. Without his stone in it."
"Get the bad thing out," I said. "And keep the rest."
She smiled. A real one. "Yes."
Somewhere over the middle of the Pacific, in the middle of the night, I woke up.
The plane was dark and humming. Everyone was asleep. Ela had her head on Uncle Tarık's shoulder. Bora was snoring with his mouth open and his crocodile neck pillow over one eye.
I looked out of the window. Far, far below, the ocean was black. Above, there were stars. Millions of them. And across the middle of the sky, the Milky Way, like a river of light.
And I could hear the winds.

Not the winds inside me. The winds outside. The winds of the Pacific. Huge and slow and ancient, sweeping across the biggest ocean in the world, the way they had for millions of years. They didn't talk much. They were too big to talk. They just moved, and hummed, like a giant breathing.
But under them, very faint, I heard something else.
Two winds. Far away. Somewhere ahead of us, in the east.
One warm and wet, like the Mediterranean. One golden, like sunrise.
The Lodos. And the Gündoğusu.
They were crying. Very quietly. Like two kids locked in a cupboard, who have been crying for so long that they're almost too tired to cry anymore.
And they were moving. Toward Mexico. In a stone hand.
*He is going to Mexico too.*
I pressed my forehead against the cold window, and I whispered, "I'm coming. Hold on. I'm coming."
I don't know if they heard me.
§END To be continued in* The Feathered Serpent...
